subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on this critical motion. The point is that the government wants to include laundry detergent in the schedule of goods which are taxed under the manufacturers' sales tax. I think it is time that we start looking at our tax system as a way to accomplish priorities that we set as a Parliament.
I believe that there is a lot of rhetoric these days about the concern regarding environmental deterioration which we see in almost every environmental area. Perhaps the government ought to give consideration to taxing only those detergents that are harmful to the environment and to giving a tax incentive for or not taxing soaps which are environmentally friendly.
In other words, if people have a choice between using detergent that will obviously harm the environment and using a detergent that is friendly to the environment in the sense that it will not do damage, why would we not then take the advantage and not tax that environmentally friendly detergent?
It would send a very clear signal that we are serious, that we are prepared to give up revenue in the hope of altering people's purchasing patterns and encouraging people to purchase environmentally friendly products and at the same time send a clear signal to those firms which are marketing goods that are in a sense against the environment to reconsider what they are doing.
It seems to me that this provides us with an excellent opportunity to send that signal, both in terms of encouraging an incentive to purchase environmentally friendly products and a signal against those firms that continue, in spite of the evidence, to market very unfriendly products.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to say a few words about this motion. I think, as my colleague from Kamloops said just a few moments ago, this is quite an opportunity for the government to actually put into action some of the things that it has been talking about.
There is very little that is more important to us than the environment right now. The point is that here we have an opportunity to actually use our tax system to promote a healthy environment here in Canada. We have a situation where the Conservative government is now asking us to include laundry detergent in the schedule of goods which are taxed under the manufacturers' sales tax provisions.
As much as we have argued in other debates in this House that the manufacturers' sales tax is a bad tax and a killer of jobs, as the Minister of Finance has indicated if it is going to amend it, it should do it in such a way that the entire country benefits since the tax itself is such a negative tax to begin with.

October 13, 1989
Government Orders
We argue that this government should tax only those products which are harmful to the environment and should in fact provide a tax incentive for those laundry detergents and other products which are environmentally friendly.
The government, I think, should increasingly be including environmental incentives in its tax policy in order to encourage companies to devise less harmful products, rather than just using the system to encourage manufacturers to do whatever they wish and to meet consumer demand.
As we know the consumers are not always correct in our system. In an economy such as ours they tend to buy the cheapest product, the product that is most easily available to them and is not always the most environmentally friendly.
This amendment before us today is a fine opportunity for us to deal with putting some action to the words that have been spoken, not just by members of the opposition but by many members of the government as well.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest and even touches of joy as the hon. Minister of the Environment stated after the last federal general election that every piece of legislation placed before this House, every element of the government's program, would be subject to rigorous testing against its environmental effects and the advisability of that program or legislation from an environmentalist point of view.
I was willing to herald this and in fact did so in my riding on a number of occasions, as a major advance by an otherwise, let us say, at best tepidly enthusiastic government at least in this regard.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: That is very generous.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
I am a generous man by nature. It is for this reason that I rise to state my certainty that this amendment will enjoy support on all sides of the House.
I cannot imagine that a government, which numbers among it so passionately eloquent and obviously dedicated a minister as is the hon. Minister of the Environment, would conduct itself in any other fashion when confronted with so sensible, reasonable and unobjectionable an amendment as that proposed by the hon. member for Yukon. It seeks to penalize no one. It seeks to prevent no consumer option. It merely attempts to foster the use by the Canadian people in one small area of a buying pattern that will be the less environmentally destructive.
Biodegradable laundry detergents are not the answer to the pollution problem in this country. By encouraging consumers to move to biodegradable laundry detergents we will not thereby have solved the environmental problems that confront this Chamber but we will have taken one small step. As the Chinese have noted a journey of a thousand li begins with a single step.
Given the pronouncements of the hon. Minister of the Environment, I assume the desires of the members opposite, and certainly those of the members on this side, I look forward to the unanimous support of this amendment in this Chamber.

The House resumed from Tuesday, October 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-18, an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to get up and speak on this bill if for no other reason than I hail from a riding and indeed a city that is in many respects a microcosm of the multicultural reality

Government Orders
which many in Canada seek to see this nation become.
Edmonton is, in the term once popularized by the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, "a community of communities". There are numerous language groups, numerous individual communities in Edmonton comprising members of cultures from around the globe, all of whom in Edmonton have come to live in a kind of harmony, a kind of over-all co-operative civic spirit that I think does the city proud and I think can act as a model for the rest of the country. This is not to say that we do not have problems in Edmonton. We do. But we have many assets in consequence of this fundamental fact.
This is most obvious in the annual heritage days festival in Edmonton. It occurs every August and is a three-day long weekend extravaganza in which the various cultures present in Edmonton get together, establish booths down in William Hawrelak Park and spend those three days marvelling at the richness and variety of each other's cultures.
I would note as well that in Edmonton, indeed in Edmonton East, there is a variety of publications in various heritage languages. We have two Italian newspapers; we have three Chinese language newspapers; we have two newspapers that are published partly in Cree; we have a Portuguese newspaper; we have a Ukrainian newspaper; and we have The Prairie Link, which is devoted to the furtherance of all these multicultural perspectives.
In the last two months I attended ceremonies to mark African Awareness Day. I attended the founding meeting of the Keiping Association of Alberta. I attended the opening of the new headquarters of the Hakka Association, and of course last summer I attended at the celebration of the Veisakha by the Sikh community in Edmonton.
This is not to say, as I noted earlier, that we are devoid of frictions in Edmonton. They are there, just as they have been there historically in Canada and I must say especially in western Canada.
There are such shameful episodes as the Komagata Maru incident, the imposition of the Chinese immigration head tax and thereafter the Immigration Exclusion Act; the systematic discrimination against Ukrainian settlers at the beginning of the century; the appalling
crimes committed against the Japanese Canadian people during the Second World War; and more recently the real racial discrimination faced by new immigrants such as the Vietnamese, the Latinos, especially Chileans and El Salvadorans, people from the Arab countries and the Sikh community.
All these are witness to the fact that racial discrimination has not been abolished from our communities, not even in a community as young and essentially open-minded as that which one will find in Edmonton.
And of course always for some reason, lurking in the background, is that particular European curse, antiSemitism, which continues to raise its ugly head from time to time in acts of vandalism in Edmonton and across Alberta.
There is no question, therefore, that in this bill we have a proposal for an act which is commendable in that it celebrates the fact of diversity in Canada and which is necessary because it seeks to foster public celebration and acceptance of that fact.
In this regard I commend, without reservation, the efforts of the government and of the minister. I note as well that on the day that this bill was moved for second reading we had the introduction of the heritage languages bill. This will create the institute, centred in Edmonton most appropriately, and is as well another commendable piece of legislation by this government. I will have more on that at second reading of that bill.
I would just like to close by noting that the term multiculturalism, that field of attitude which is intended to cover the openness of spirit, generosity and goodwill expressed toward people who are apparently different from us or toward people who apparently pursue different cultural values, is and always has been a fundamental precept of the party of which I am proud to be a member.
From the days in which the CCF opposed the Exclusion Act in B.C. and from the days in which the CCF opposed the relocation of Japanese Canadians in the Second World War to the present, our party has always stood for justice for and a welcoming of people from around the world into the project that is the building of the Canadian nation.
In some senses this was best expressed by our founding leader James Shaver Woodsworth who concluded his grace before meat with the words: "What we desire for
October 13, 1989
ourselves we wish for all." That is the spirit that animates this bill, and I celebrate it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned with amazement and indignation of the resolution proposed by aldermen Darrel Kent, Jac-quelin Holzman and Michael McSweeney and passed by a committee of the City of Ottawa to abolish the French services advisory board.
This reprisal for Bill 178 is frightfully and unacceptably cynical. Nothing is more vicious and two-faced than an elected bigot who holds a minority group hostage and punishes, or seeks to punish, it for an action beyond its control and for which it is in no way responsible.
In the capital of this country which should reflect Canada's linguistic duality, tolerance and generosity, it is unacceptable for some city councillors to show such ignorance, narrow-mindedness and intolerance.
Mr. Speaker, if these elected representatives of the people are unable to act with dignity and understanding, they should resign and be replaced!

Mr. Speaker, national unity is one of the most important topics of our time. Our challenge as Canadians is to find a balance between our need to express our uniqueness and our need to identify with the common national purpose.
It is important to express our individuality. It is important to show others what makes us special as Canadians. In some cases it may also be appropriate to promote the differences among us. Indeed, most Canadians will agree that it is our differences that have in fact given our country its strength.
However, rather than dwelling on our differences let us focus instead on what makes us the same as Canadians. Now is the time to celebrate our national identity. Now is the time to work together in the national interest. Let us all work together to face the economic challenges in Canada.

October 13, 1989
Let us work together as one Canada to build a better future for our children. Let us all, Canadians from sea to sea, work together to build a better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize an El Salvadoran woman of courage and dedication, Magdalena Hernandez, who is currently visiting Canada.
Ms. Hernandez is a member of the village council and president of the women's council of the village of Las Vueltas in El Salvador. Ten years ago the people of many villages in El Salvador, including Las Vueltas, fled their homes because of bombings and death squads.
Two years ago today these refugees started returning to their homes from the Honduras refugee camps, from San Salvador and elsewhere. Indeed, just next week over 1,600 people will be going back to their home villages from the refugee camp of Mesa Grande, which I had the privilege of visiting last month. This will be the fourth return of these people.
Given the increasing level of violence in El Salvador since Christiani came to power, I call upon the Government of Canada to support these people in their courageous return. I call upon the Government of Canada to condemn the human rights violations which have been taking place in El Salvador, the wave of assassinations, of abductions, of disappearances.
Finally, I urge our government to call upon the United Nations to provide all the necessary support so that the people of Las Vueltas and the people of other villages throughout El Salvador can join with courageous villagers, such as Magdalena Hernandez who is in the gallery, today in rebuilding a new El Salvador, an El Salvador of peace, an El Salvador of democracy and of justice.

Mr. Speaker, this week witnessed an historic moment in this chamber when His Majesty King Hussein of Jordan became the first head of state of an Arab country to address both Houses of the Canadian Parliament.
Those of us who have favoured dialogue and promoted moderation were particularly impressed with the eloquent, reasonable and pragmatic approach to peace outlined by our guest.
I also commend our Prime Minister for reiterating Canada's support for the concept of land for peace.
To bring peace to a region fraught with violence, the voices of moderation such as those of King Hussein deserve our unconditional support.
The peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the crux of the problem, can be attained by the creation of an independent Palestinian state to complement all of the others in the region.

Mr. Speaker, a secret document prepared for the Premier of Nova Scotia is nothing short of a scathing indictment of this government's policies on regional development and its pure deception in trying to mislead the people of Atlantic Canada about the activities of ACOA.
On May 17 the minister responsible for ACOA told a Commons committee that ACOA had spent nearly $600 million in Atlantic Canada. This claim was repeated on July 4 by the then president of ACOA, and again on October 6 by the minister responsible.
However, this confidential document that I have clearly shows that the actual investment by ACOA was some 40 per cent less than that claimed by the minister and this government. The credibility of this minister and the ACOA officials is now being seriously questioned as is this government's stated commitment to regional development. To quote from the premier's document: "At the moment, Atlantic Canada is practically depraved of incentives to attract industry and investment-this is not acceptable and cannot continue. We demand equal fair treatment in this Confederation".
I now call upon this government to initiate a full public inquiry into the operations of ACOA and this government's actions, not rhetoric, as it relates to regional economic development.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the announcement of VIA's new reference levels, the 11 government members of southwestern and western Ontario have consistently and unrelentlessly asserted the importance of passenger rail service for our area.
The retention of both the north and south line routes in southwestern Ontario as part of VIA's new national network has reaffirmed this importance for both my riding of Sarnia-Lambton and southwestern Ontario in general.
In my riding a group of community representatives have already taken another step forward. Rather than dwell on the supposed demise of passenger rail services, they have become involved in a local task force to help ascertain what type of new schedule and equipment could best address the area's travelling needs. Coupled with my personal meeting with VIA officials, I believe that this group will provide a valuable forum through which viable suggestions can be offered for optimal local passenger rail service.
The efforts of this task force, I think, are both timely and constructive. Certainly they demonstrate that some are fully committed to a national and local rail system that is sustainable and affordable, and one that can be built upon in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to urge the government to meet the needs of Canadian children by approving the funding application for the Kids' Help Phone.
Since May, this line has handled 45,000 calls from children across the country. More than 3,000 calls have been from children reporting abuse. More than 1,300 calls have been threats of suicide.
Without federal funds, the Kids' Help Phone is in jeopardy. At first they requested $1.3 million. Now they need $2 million just to keep up. Meetings with the Minister of National Health and Welfare have resulted in nothing.
Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting that the government can get off lightly in its responsibility to Canadian kids by only providing funds for this one help line. What this line tells us is that there is a desperate need for more services for our children, especially in rural, remote and isolated areas.
If this govenment can spend millions to advertise the trade deal, $2.7 million to advertise its budget and take out full page ads to laud a tax bill not yet passed by Parliament, then surely it can provide money to a service responding to the pleas for help from our children.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to Michel Juneau of Val d'Or. In 1982, 3,000 feet underground, the platform on which he was working gave way and Michel fell 50 feet. This accident was to change his life painfully: at 27, he became a paraplegic.
Recently, he confided that the first year was the hardest. "Still wearing pyjamas at five in the afternoon is not living. I had to get out of my shell." That is what he did. He regained his taste for sport with the Val d'Or Passe-partout, a wheelchair basketball club.
In the most recent Canadian championships on June 18 in Winnipeg, he finished only 26 seconds behind Andre Viger. On November 5, he will be at the world championships in Japan, but Michel says: What I am proudest of is not the victories and the travel. It is rather that I managed as a disabled person to join the rest of society. Most people now see me as a real athlete.
Mr. Speaker, that is a true champion and a model of perseverance!
 * *

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are misreading the intentions of the South African government to provide real change in South Africa.

October 13, 1989
The Canadian government should not let up on the pressure just because South Africa is talking a good story. There must be some real change.
Canada, by not proposing new sanctions in Kuala Lumpur, is telling the world that South Africa is prepared to make changes. I ask the Prime Minister, where are these real changes? Actions speak louder than words. Real change would be to release all political prisoners and to say when there will be real elections in South Africa.
The Prime Minister has advocated total economic sanctions against South Africa if it did not make progress toward dismantling apartheid. This government should show real leadership and call for more sanctions to show the South African government that it will not accept petty apartheid talk as concrete indications of its willingness to make real change in South Africa.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's first hotline for troubled children, the Kids' Help Phone, averages 800 calls a day. These calls range from suicide threats, fights with their parents, teen pregnancies and many other problems associated with being a troubled child.
Kids' Help Phone will have to end its service if this government does not come through with a $1.3 million dollar grant by the end of the month.
The best statement department officials could make was that the proposal was under review. Is the government reviewing whether the little girl who gets beaten by her drunk parents needs help, whether the teenager who finds out she is pregnant and has no where to turn needs advice, or whether the young boy who is having problems dealing with the fear of drug addiction needs guidance? Or is it reviewing whether $1.3 million is too high a price to pay to reach the seven million children in Canada?
Kids' Help Phone needs the government's help. Kids in this country need the government's help. I urge this government not to let them down.

Mr. Speaker, during hearings of Bill C-21 by the unemployment insurance committee much rhetoric was heard from opponents about money being taken out of the UI system.
In fact, this money is being reinvested to assist unemployed or laid-off Canadians to prepare for, find and achieve full-time permanent employment, something for which this government has an enviable and impressive record.
In particular, 50 million additional dollars will go for the Community Futures Program and 15 million additional dollars for the industrial adjustment service. Used this way, these funds represent a valuable, long-term benefit for currently unemployed Canadians.
I urge the government to target much of these additional funds for use in areas hit hard by the downturn in the Atlantic fishery or impacted by base closures. In particular, I urge the immediate designation of Shelburne and Queens counties in Nova Scotia for the Community Futures Program.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in my office I received a telephone call from a farmer who works in northwest Saskatchewan near The Battlefords. He told me to pass a message to the government across the way. He said he is a long-time Conservative who is now a former supporter of the government party.
The government, he said, has forgotten about the farmer. Grain is not moving from the elevators. He cannot sell his grain and his debts have to be paid. The situation leaves him in a heck of a spot.
If the government realized the true situation, it would maintain the cash advance payments for grain. The cash advance is not a loan and should not be subject to the interest payments. The program was put in place to provide payments for grain, some of which cannot be sold because quotas are off or elevators are plugged.
October 13, 1989

If this government wants to help western farmers, it would bring forth the statutes under the existing legislation to allow advance payments to be made and at the same time bring in legislation to reduce interest rates for all farm loans for Canadian farmers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday 2,700 workers at the General Motors plant in Scarborough were told by the company that the plant's operations are under review.
I contacted General Motors last night to express my concern about this announcement. I will be holding further meetings with their officials early next week.
The General Motors plant has been an important part of Scarborough's economy for over 35 years. In that time it has changed its production lines three times. However, yesterday's announcement has raised serious concerns among the workers and their families about the status of the plant.
In my meetings with General Motors I will urge the company to work closely with the workers to ensure that the Scarborough facility remains an important part of our community.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday a committee of three aldermen of the City of Ottawa, three well-known Conservatives, including the "babysitter" alderman Michael McSween-ey, passed a resolution to eliminate the city's advisory committee on official languages.
Mr. Speaker, this gesture was apparently as a form of reprisal against the Quebec National Assembly's passage of Bill 178.
Ottawa is the capital of our country and as such has an important role to play in preserving and promoting Canadian unity.
Mr. Speaker, I want to appeal to all Members in the House of Commons and all my colleagues at the provincial and municipal levels in the National Capital Region to dissociate themselves from the comments made by the three aldermen. I think it is high time the Prime Minister told his friend Michael McSweeney about Canada's linguistic duality.

Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport is in the House.
Next week at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers meeting there will be an opportunity for the Government of Canada to persuade other governments in the Commonwealth to follow the sports policy that this government has introduced in respect of apartheid in South Africa. I would urge the government to use this opportunity and to ensure that from here on the Commonwealth Games are boycott free.

Mr. Speaker, Canada must adjust to current economic conditions and adopt a fair taxation system. Our new approach to taxation must include changes in the present federal sales tax. This is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had in mind when he proposed a new sales tax system called the goods and services tax. It is widely agreed that our present system, which puts a 13.5 per cent tax on most products manufactured and purchased in Canada, no longer reflects the economic situation in this country. The tax is obsolete and is detrimental to business development.
The system proposed by our government is modem, more flexible, and, most important, takes into account the situation of senior citizens and families on incomes below $30,000 annually. Mr. Speaker, it is clear the new system must be implemented as soon as possible.

Eighty per cent of Canadians don't agree.

October 13, 1989
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I will pose my question to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion.
We learned yesterday that 2,500 jobs at the General Motors plant in Scarborough, plus hundreds more in the auto parts industry that supplies that factory, are now being put on the chopping block as a direct consequence of the free trade agreement.
Oh, oh!
I want to point out to the House that the loss of 2,500 jobs is no laughing matter. The Tories should not laugh about it.
Hear, hear!
I want to ask the minister a very simple question. What does the government intend to do to prevent the loss of these jobs in the vital auto industry in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first point out that in automobiles there has been free trade since 1965.
In the last few years this particular company has invested about $8 million in Canada, quite a lot of it in the constituency of the member for Oshawa. This is a van production facility. There were two equal sized facilities, one in Ohio and one in Scarborough, which they are phasing out.
Guess which one they're keeping open.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
They are closing both of them, as a matter of fact. They are closing both lines and consolidating in Flint, Michigan. In the meantime, they are looking for an alternate product line to produce in Scarborough.
What happened yesterday was the prudent kind of indication to employees that changes are coming. But that is a part of the operations of this company which has been operating under free trade since 1965, much to Canada's benefit.
Mr. Axworthy (Winnipeg South Centre) Mr. Speaker, I want to simply point out to the minister that there was an auto pact in this country. It is this government that removed the safeguards and removed the tariffs. It is this government that is responsible for the loss of jobs.
As a consequence, we want to know from this government what proposals it is going to make at the automobile working group. Is it supporting a 60 per cent content rule? What proposals will the government make to provide for the protection and enhancement of jobs in the vital automobile industry?
This government has the responsibility. This government has to take some action. This government cannot avoid the basic consequence that it signed a rotten deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
If the hon. member is assigning responsibility for these things, presumably he will equally assign credit to this government for the over million and a half jobs generated. Surely he will assign credit to this government for the tremendous automobile trade surplus we have been enjoying and continue to enjoy because of the policies of this government. Perhaps he will recognize all of those factors.
As his colleague and former finance critic had indicated, the Liberals will attempt to blame every sparrow that falls on the free trade agreement. This is another attempt in this regard.
I remind him again, in terms of trade in automobiles, the operation of the automobile industry, the rules in place today have been in place since 1965.

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The Minister says there will be more jobs. However, according to the report based on serious studies on free trade conducted by this Government, and according to other studies by the private sector, and also according to the Canadian Labour Congress, 60,000 jobs have already been lost as a result of free trade. When will this Government start taking seriously the right of Canadians to know what the consequences are of free trade? I request a public examination by Parliament on the subject of free trade and Canadians jobs.
October 13, 1989

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and Shirley Carr are surely the only two people in Canada who take that list and those numbers seriously. That was a pathetic, ridiculous list. I am surprised that an aspirant to the leadership of his party would be so naive as to repeat those numbers.
Where are your studies?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Our studies show that since free trade was introduced, the number of new jobs created in Canada is 189,000. The hon. member over there is talking about the studies. These are Statistics Canada numbers. These are not inventions of Shirley Carr. They are Statistics Canada numbers.
Are they your invention?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: The numbers indicate the economy is continuing to percolate along, as it has over the last five years. As long as we are saved from the kinds of policies the hon. member would introduce, the economy will continue to percolate along.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a question for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. I want to say to him that his words are no consolation for the 2,500 Canadian workers in Scarborough who are going to lose their jobs because of the government's lack of commitment and action.
I also want to say this to the minister: Does he not realize he is not here to make excuses for General Motors? I ask the minister, therefore, why will he not make a commitment today to preserve those 2,500 jobs at Scarborough? Why will he not on behalf of the government stand up today for Canada and Canadian workers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what happened yesterday was a corporation, General Motors, indicated that it is changing the production because of changing markets, because of changing needs in its company. The vans that had been produced there and in Ohio in roughly equal numbers will no longer be produced. They informed their employees of that fact. They are looking for other operations.
Oral Questions
General Motors is well aware, as are most Canadians, that Canadian auto workers are very productive. In fact, that is the reason we enjoy a tremendous surplus in automobile trade with the United States.
General Motors has a facility there with very productive workers. It is searching for a replacement for the van. It is in their interests to find that replacement.
I do not know why the hon. member feels it is appropriate today to do the Chicken Little routine and say the sky is falling. It may not be falling.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this government came into office and before this minister became the minister, the automotive industry was sufficiently competitive that jobs were moving to Canada and staying in Canada.

I want to ask the Minister to acknowledge that since the Government's free trade agreement was implemented, we have lost jobs and plants to the United States. Why won't the Government admit today that the Free Trade Agreement is a disaster for our country?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate is lower than it has been for some eight or nine years. Since January there have been 189,000 new jobs created in Canada to add on to the over 1.5 million over the last four years. I realize that it is disappointing news to the opposition to have the economy continue to perform that way, but we do not think that is disappointing news.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. I choose my words with care. Just a minute ago he misled the House. I want to find out if he did it deliberately or inadvertently. I want to give him a chance to clear the record.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Order.

That is perfectly in order. I want the minister to clarify it.
He said that we are operating under the same rules today as we were in 1965. In 1965 investment requirements were established in Canada for U.S. firms in this industry to make sure we got our jobs. As a result of the free trade agreement in place now, those investment requirements are gone. That is to say the rules are

October 13, 1989
Oral Questions
different today because of what the Conservative Government did than what they were in 1965.
Will the minister confirm that the rules have changed, that there are no longer Canadian investment requirements, and that they have been removed by this government? Second, what is to prevent in the future GM, Chrysler in Brampton or Ford in Oakville from moving lock, stock and barrel if it is in their financial interest out of Canada into the U.S. as a result of the removal of the investment safeguards by the Conservative Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate was had last year. We went over it ad nauseam last year.
The hon. member is talking about safeguards which are so far away from the reality today as to be totally meaningless. That debate was held last year. The people decided. I do not understand. Is he a sore loser? Why does he keep coming back to something that is over and done with and established?
He surely is not claiming that the decisions announced yesterday had anything to do with that safety mechanism that was there in 1965 which was proven to be unnecessary, irrelevant and totally divorced from the reality of what is going on.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows that his own government ministers since 1984 have cited the investment requirements-they used to-and correctly pointed out that General Motors normally exceeded the requirements. Now that the government has removed the requirements they pretend they are useless.
I want to ask the minister this. Given the great rationalization that is going on in that industry throughout this continent, why should any Canadian now working in the industry, and there are over 100,000, believe that when future investment decisions are made, whether by General Motors, Chrysler or Ford, that these investments will take place in Canada? They are no longer required to do it. Immense political pressure is building up in the U.S. Why, I ask again, will the industry-given the choice between expanding in Canada and the U.S.-not move to the U.S.? What is going to keep those jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member is not suggesting that the $8 billion of investment by
General Motors was because of the safeguards and I hope he will agree with me that that money was invested by GM because it recognized that Canadian workers are very productive, that it can make a good profit margin on production in Canada. That is why it made the investment.
The hon. member seems to suggest the only way we can keep investment in Canada is by putting up barriers and forcing people to stay. Today's The Globe and Mail has an interesting article which states: "Freightliner Canada Ltd. plans to build a freight truck assembly plant in the southwestern city of St. Thomas and should eventually employ up to 1,200 people". They are not forced to do that. They are doing it because it makes good sense to them. Those 1,200 people are going to appreciate the work.

Mr. Speaker, today it was reported that Chiysler, which currently has plants in Brampton, is about to make a decision to transfer its production to the United States within a few years. My question to the Minister is quite straightforward: Tuesday, the Government refused to entertain the findings of to studies on the impact of the FTA on employment in this major industry. Would the Minister be prepared to talk directly to the presidents of Chiysler, General Motors and Ford about their intentions for the future, in order to protect investment and employment here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have an ongoing dialogue with the automobile industry, both the big assembler and the pack-parts companies and so on, to ensure that Canada remains a good place to do business and to ensure that they continue to invest here. The success of those kinds of discussions is evidenced by the tremendous investment we have had in this industry. For instance there is the indication from Freightliner of a new truck assembly plant in Canada. We will continue to do that in the future.
I would ask the hon. member to have more confidence in Canadians, we can compete. We have shown in the past and we will show it in the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of the Environment, the minister who is acting on behalf of Canadians.
This week we learned that contaminants which potentially cause cancer and brain damage are being found in the Great Lakes. The situation is so serious that the minister of health himself pointed to problems with foetuses, native populations and others.
Can the Acting Minister of the Environment explain who in the federal government authorized the dredging in the St. Clair River, the dumping of contaminants which are potential cancer causing contaminants directly into the open waters? Who authorized that and why was there not an environmental assessment done?

Mr. Speaker, some of these questions were raised yesterday and it was pointed out that the government has acted, monitoring has taken place. The results of this monitoring process, which has been ongoing for some time, does not give rise to the kind of alarmist statements that have been made by the hon. member and by others. In fact, one of the authors of the report pointed to the need for further research before some of these so-called health effects can be substantiated.
It would behove us to get behind the new programs that have been worked out with American jurisdictions, the provinces and municipalities in the area and, indeed, the industry, to make sure that the $125 million that has been announced to address some of these questions; the health effects, remedial action and preventive action, is used to lever similar initiatives from other jurisdictions and that we get on with job.

Mr. Speaker, Canada was embarrassed on the international stage yesterday when the Council of Three Fires of Walpole Island told the IJC that they are forced to take the Canadian Government to court to stop the dumping of hundreds of contaminants, which have the potential to cause cancer and brain damage, in the drinking water of approximately 45 million people living on the Canadian and American sides of the border.
Oral Questions
I would like to ask the Acting Minister of the Environment; who authorized the open dumping of the contaminants that are now being dumped by the Canadian Government, by the Department of Public Works, into the St. Clair River? Who authorized that and who is going to take the responsibility for the potential health damages?
Mr. Speaker, I can tell the hon. member that my colleague the minister who-
He's in Paris.

-is on an urgent trip to Europe to consult with environment ministers there. She herself would admit that the issue of the environment is a global issue, an international issue. We are recognized as having assumed a leadership role in certain critical areas. My colleague would want to verify the evidence that has been induced before we would want to examine it any further.
It's in the courts.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. In Newfoundland there are approximately 49,000 homes without adequate water or sewers. This will only be remedied if $1.3 billion is found.
Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware of raw sewage being dumped into lakes, rivers and harbours across Canada and would his government today, in this House, make a financial commitment to Canadians to address this potential environmental disaster as recommended by the Institute for Research and Public Policy?

Mr. Speaker, the government is aware of situations where municipal sewers are discharged into harbours and into other environments. I can tell the hon. member that, yes, we take this situation very seriously. We have signalled our concerns to the provinces and municipalities which have the principal responsibility for the clean-up and the adherence to the environmental standards that we have already.

Mr. Speaker, using the minister's own words that the provinces and the municipalities should pay for the repairs of their sewage systems, where does he

October 13, 1989
Oral Questions
expect the people of Newfoundland to come up with $1,300,000 to repair their sewer systems? The total package is $5.7 billion to repair the sewage systems in Newfoundland. Where does he expect the people of Newfoundland to come up with that kind of money?

I do
not want to appear flippant or parenthetical about my answer, but the people of Newfoundland have the same sources to come up with money as has the federal government. As the hon. member knows, we are in a very tight fiscal situation. Unfortunately, there is only one source of money and that is the taxpayers of Canada. We are dipping into the same pocket that the province of Newfoundland would have to dip into.
I should, however, point out to the hon. member that there are programs that the federal government has engaged in with the province of Newfoundland, such as transfer payments and other assistance, that help the provinces to maintain certain minimum standards that are desirable throughout our country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Housing. Yesterday the minister announced the release of federal lands at Vaughan near Toronto for housing.
The minister indicated that only 25 per cent or 600 units of the 2,500 homes, will be affordable housing. Is the minister aware that already this morning four respected Toronto housing groups have, in a press statement, criticized him for not specifying how many co-operative and non-profit housing units will be built. Will the minister now tell this House how many nonprofit and co-operative housing units will be built on the lands at Vaughan?

Mr. Speaker, as I am sure the hon. member is well aware, the whole process of developing land for housing entails the putting together of a plan of development and the obtaining of approval of that plan from the local municipality and all of the other authorities that are involved in that process.
Obviously until the firm plan is settled and has been worked out with the town of Vaughan, the region of York and the province of Ontario, it is impossible to designate specifically where the housing that will be available for
non-profit groups and for co-operative housing groups will be located.
But we are committed to providing a minimum of 25 per cent affordable housing in accordance with the province of Ontario's guidelines. We will be doing our best to maximize the amounts available not only for first-time home buyers but also for the non-profit groups.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is aware that the 25 per cent affordable housing provision is simply the minimum requirement of Ontario. Why is the minister acting like any other developer? He is only doing what is required by Ontario. How can he justify a policy that subsidizes the rich and slams the door on the poor?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has stated, the 25 per cent is indeed a minimum. That is what the announcement I made yesterday indicated, that it certainly was a minimum and that we were going to do our best to make sure that it was much higher than that. Affordable housing, in the definition of the province of Ontario, does not just include non-profit and co-op housing but, of course, includes housing for first time home buyers.
We would hope that we would be able to maximize the number of homes available for first time home buyers and also for the social housing groups as well. I am sure the hon. member and all Canadians will be most happy when this development has been built and completed.

Mr. Speaker, the finance committee is currently holding hearings in Ottawa and across the country on the goods and services tax. These have been and continue to be very productive meetings across the country. However, rumours and reports today indicated that the Minister of Finance is about to introduce GST legislation. Would the minister assure the House that this is merely a draft bill for discussion purposes?

Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that to the hon. member. We are proposing only to release draft legislation. The draft will put into legal language a number of elements that were set out in the technical paper. We have been encouraged to do this by the chairman of the finance committee, as my colleague fully understands, as well as by the legal and accounting communities who are anxious to see what

the legal words of the technical requirements of the proposal are so that they can make specific comments on the technical aspects of the proposed bill.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Minister of National Defence quoted a statement from an editorial in the Summerside Journal-Pioneer to support his decision to close CFB Summerside. It was a misrepresentation of the newspaper's position and the minister knew it. He also deliberately misled the House when he quoted these-
Order.

-search and rescue statistics.
A statement from the Journal-Pioneer last Tuesday really demonstrates how the paper feels, and I quote: "Defence Minister Bill McKnight has displayed both arrogance and truculence while questioned in the House. But he added a new ingredient during Question Period on Friday, deception".
Will the minister apologize to the Journal-Pioneer for his misleading statements of last Friday. Will he stop playing politics with people's lives, and will he open a public inquiry to determine what the real situation is in regard to search and rescue?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want some clarification from the hon. member who just put the question. I heard "misleading". I did not hear "deliberately". I want a clarification of that.
He said "deliberately".
I want an apology, not a clarification.
Oh sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: How about Prince Edward Island?

Now you're being arrogant and truculent again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, I would like to know what the hon. member said and then I will decide whether there should be an apology.
If I used the word "deliberately", I did not mean it, but I did mean "misleading".

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: You said he knowingly mislead the House. That's what you said.
Well he did.
You have it written down right on your notes. Liar. You have it written down on your notes.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I serve notice now that I will raise a question of privilege at the conclusion of Question Period.
He has it written down.

The hon. member suggests that I misled the House. Mr. Speaker, the article is under the heading called "Editorial", located where the editorial is usually located in the Journal-Pioneer. It was not an Op-Ed. There was no attribution to another newspaper that would suggest that this was not. What it does say is: "It is unfortunate, however, that one shall benefit-" There is one line, "but we are ready to receive it nevertheless, says the Halifax Chronicle-Herald."
This does not say in any way that it was an editorial reprinted from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. It says,
It is unfortunate, however, that one shall benefit while another suffers. Nova Scotia did not seek the major source of Summerside's pride and economic support, but we are ready to receive it nevertheless, says the Halifax Chronicle-Herald.
What I am saying and what I will continue to say-
Apologize.

Hon. members are yelling "apologize". If I implied there was any intent to the lack of editorial integrity or the lack of editorial ability by the Summer-side Pioneer-Journal, which has to take an editorial and place it as an editorial from another newspaper, I apologize.
What I would like to say to the hon. member and to the people of Summerside is, this decision was not an easy decision. This decision was made because $2.74 billion was reduced from the defence department's

Oral Questions
budget. The $2.74 billion meant we had to change what we were doing. Operational efficiencies have not been jeopardized. A savings of some $900 million will be acquired by the Government of Canada over the next 15 years to use in the security of Canada through the Department of National Defence.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who is also the chairperson of the federal-provincial task force looking into the closure of CFB Summerside.
Since the announcement of the closure approximately six months ago, the economy of Summerside and area has been devastated, mainly due to lack of confidence. Immediate action is required. The people of Summer-side need a real federal commitment, otherwise the damage may be irreversible. When is the minister going to make an announcement that will provide jobs and will restore the much needed confidence within the community?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question. We have been working very hard on this issue, together with the province.
We have three federal-provincial working groups looking at alternate uses of the physical assets of CFB Summerside, potential alternate public sector activities for the Summerside area, on which I am working very closely with my colleagues here, and industrial incentives and activities necessary to attract private sector investment to Summerside.
I have had two meetings of the federal-provincial joint committee with Mr. Morrissey. The task forces have been meeting and Mr. Morrissey and I will be meeting again in the very near future to discuss our progress.
Like the hon. member, I am anxious to work with the province so that the two of us can come up with something that will be helpful to the future of Summer-side.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
In prisons across Canada over 1,000 workers, including correction services officers, parole officers, recreation and training programmers have been without a contract for over two years. Next Friday they will be in a legal position to strike, erecting picket lines that guards will not cross. With the security of Canadian prisons at stake, why has the minister let things get so far out of hand, and what will the minister do now to settle this lengthy dispute?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we negotiated in good faith with all the groups in the Public Service Alliance of Canada and reached a settlement that was not ratified by this particular group of some 1,500 employees. They elected to ask the PSSRB to appoint a conciliation board. That conciliation board has yet to report, and until it does, I think it would be inappropriate for me to give a government response to a report that we have yet to receive.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member did not ask for a response to the report, the member asked for action. My supplementary question is directed to the Solicitor General.
If these workers do go on strike, as may happen, 8,000 parolees will be without supervision in towns and cities all across Canada. Inmates in prisons will be without training or recreational opportunities and, in my view, lives will be endangered. When is the minister going to act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can say that Correctional Services Canada is well aware of the situation. We are waiting for the report, as my colleague, the President of Treasury Board said earlier. We already have a contingency plan, which includes the assistance of police authorities, to ensure the security of Canadians, because the security of our citizens is paramount. Furthermore, my officials, both at Correctional Services and those involved in the contingency plan, have assured me that in any case, if anything happens and people cannot be supervised in the usual way, the security of our citizens will be guaranted at all times, Mr. Speaker.
October 13, 1989

Mr. Speaker, late last week the Alberta government decided to step in and clean up the mess left by Peter Pocklington at his Gainers meat packing plant in Edmonton. At least 1,200 jobs have been saved.
Now we read where Bill Janklow, the former governor of South Dakota, and the man who called out the state troopers to block Canadian hogs from his state, says this bail-out is countervailable under the free trade agreement. He wants new duties imposed against Canadian hogs. And the American National Pork Producers Council is watching.
In the absence of the Minister for International Trade my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. What is the government going to do to let our American cousins know, with all due respect, that actions taken by our governments to preserve our meat packing industry and the jobs of hundreds of our citizens is none of their business?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is aware that there is, at the present time, a 3.6 cent per pound countervail that has been imposed as a result of a countervail claim that was made by the United States of America. That issue is being fought by the Canadian Government and by the pork producers and the Meat Council of Canada through two specific areas, through the GATT and through section 19 of the free trade agreement.
Thanks to the free trade agreement, we have an opportunity now to deal with this dispute in an objective and an impartial way, and I am confident about the outcome.
The fact that the Alberta government has taken over Gainers certainly has no bearing upon this at this particular time. Just because there has been a change in ownership, I do not believe that would constitute an action for countervail.

Mr. Speaker, thanks to the free trade agreement, as the minister well knows, we have the opportunity now to find out whether or not the Americans are applying their own law fairly
Oral Questions
according to their law. He knows, further, that especially the $10 million guarantee that the Alberta government is giving to Gainers is precisely that which, among others, the American Pork Producers Council is considering as to whether or not it is countervailable.
Again I ask the minister. What is this government going to do to stick up for Canadian jobs in Canadian meat packing plants against the predations of Americans?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, I am making progress, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member now says the American government is considering. It is quite well in order for producers in America to make representations to their government, as producers in Canada make representations to this government.
The producers in this country know very well that this government stands up for them, and we are working together in fighting this issue. It is based upon a GATT decision but fortunately we have a free trade dispute resolving mechanism which will be more effective, more impartial, more objective, and more successful.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade but, in his absence, I will address it to the minister responsible for small business and tourism.
There is considerable concern among lobster fishermen in southern Nova Scotia about a protectionist piece of legislation now before the U.S. Congress and supported by Senate majority leader George Mitchell of Maine, that could block the export of Nova Scotia lobsters to the United States.
Clearly the bill represents a trade distorting action that violates both the GATT and the free trade agreement. What action is the Government of Canada prepared to take to protect Nova Scotia's $100 million lobster industry?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

Mr. Speaker, in reply to my hon. friend, I remind him that of course this is just a proposal. It is not a passed piece of legislation. It is a proposal which we find objectionable on scientific grounds. We also find it objectionable in terms of enforcement. We do not find it consistent at all with GATT or with the FTA and we

October 13, 1989

delivered a message to that effect a week ago today. We will continue to pursue this very vigorously.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for the status of women. In June, 1988 this government committed $40 million to a so-called family violence initiative. Twenty-two million dollars of this was to go to CMHC for something called Project Haven. As of 9.30 this morning, 16 months later, the total moneys taken up in Project Haven amount to $803,120 for a total of 20 rooms.
One million Canadian women can expect to be assaulted in this country in the near future. Could the minister tell us how much good she thinks 20 rooms will do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we commissioned a report which was released at the meeting in Montreal. We find it very helpful in aiding our understanding and raising awareness of the issue. We share the very serious concerns that the authors have raised and we will use our program effectively in combating those most disturbing attitudes and practices.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that is very reassuring to the one in four women in this country who are assaulted before the age of 17.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women says that workers against family violence across this country are saying, "Where is the money, what has been done with the other $18 million?"
My question again is for the minister responsible for the status of women. Would she commit herself to report to the House what is being done with this money, can we see where the money is going and can we do something rather than raise the awareness? The awareness is there. Let us have some action and let us see where the dollars are.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern, and I think that she knows it is shared by myself and the members of this government.
The $40 million that we announced in June, 1988 was the largest single increase ever in funding on family violence issues. There are a variety of components in it, as well as public awareness. I will be veiy happy to look into the particular issue that she has raised, and she knows that I have done that before and will continue to do it.
However, I do want the House to know that this government has made very strong efforts on behalf of the women who face these very terrible difficulties.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Recent cut-backs to VIA Rail services, combined with curtailment of other railway activities, intentionally promoted by this government in the past have caused undue hardship throughout my province of New Brunswick and Canada.
If the government persists with these actions, can the minister explain what economic adjustment programs will be put in place to assist communities and those segments of the population, like senior citizens and students, which will be severely affected by these cutbacks?

Mr. Speaker, indeed the government is aware of the different applications of decisions that we have made. We have at different levels and different departments, like employment and immigration, regional development, ACOA, and so on, different ways in which we will be able to help people.
However, I do not believe that it is basically something which has anything to do with the cuts at VIA Rail. I believe, once again, that the decision has been made in the best interest, and if there are any hardships anywhere, they will be considered under all government programs.
October 13, 1989

I have a supplementary question. New Brunswick needs financial assistance from the federal government to repair and improve its highway system, which is in pitiful condition.
Following the VIA Rail cuts, can the Minister explain to us what he intends to do to help New Brunswick and the other provinces whose highway systems are in the same deplorable condition?

Mr. Speaker, I think that my colleague is aware that Canada's highway system is in provincial jurisdiction. So the responsibility for such an initiative rests with the province of New Brunswick.
However, at the last meeting of provincial transport ministers and myself a few weeks ago in Calgary, we decided to continue work on a national highway polity. We are at the third stage of determining some technical points.
Obviously, the federal government in its present financial condition cannot make any commitment to give money to the provinces.
Nevertheless, as this policy is developed, some points are taken into consideration and I think that when the time comes, we will be able to have the necessary discussions.
Once again, I do not want to leave the impression that we will invest any money, for now. We cannot afford it. We will continue to work with the provinces, as was agreed in Calgary in September.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I have a copy of a study done by Tristad Resources based on a Statistics Canada model. It shows that after one year of GST,
100.000	poor people who got the tax credit the first year will receive nothing in terms of a tax credit and after five years of operation, because of partial indexation, some
400.000	families will not receive a tax credit.
Oral Questions
What I want to know from the Minister of Finance is whether or not he will confirm those figures and that because of partial indexation the poor people of this country, some 100,000 families, after one year will receive nothing, and after five years 400,000 families will receive nothing from this Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, let us start from ground zero. When we came into office there were no refundable sales tax credits to low income Canadians to offset the burden of sales tax. We introduced a refundable sales tax credit in 1986. We increased the threshold from $15,000 to $16,000 a year later-to $18,000 recently-and it will be going to $25,000 with the introduction of the goods and services tax.
I think the hon. member will acknowledge, I am sure, that the number of people who will be receiving this sales tax credit has increased considerably over the years and will increase even more as we move toward the introduction of the goods and services tax.
Just to put a dollar amount on this, the federal sales tax credit is $1.2 billion now and will be $3.6 billion with the introduction of the goods and services tax credit.

Mr. Speaker, the refusal of the minister to answer the question of course confirms that the GST means that after five years
400,000	families that are poor will lose the entire tax credit, and another 300,000 families will lose part of their tax credit.
I want to know from this Minister of Finance why he is taking a mean spirited approach in attacking poor people in this country by introducing the GST which will take money out of their pockets.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how he can characterize me as being mean spirited when I have been at the heart of the introduction of the refundable sales tax credit that is providing the offset to those people in low income brackets.
Now in specific response to the question, surely he understands that we review these matters, these thresholds on a regular basis. As I have indicated, the threshold was originally $15,000, then we increased it to $16,000, then to $18,000, and with the goods and services tax credit we will be proposing to increase it to $25,000. With the amount of people who are benefiting from the reform of the income tax system as a result of the review

Privilege
of the thresholds at which people start paying tax,
850,000	Canadians were taken off the tax rolls. This is an indication of how this government is responding to the needs of low income Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to ask the House and to ask you to review a question that was put by the hon. member for Egmont. He is a member with whom I have no difficulty in putting forward the cause of his constituents and those who sent him to this House. However, in suggesting when reading from an editorial of September 26 from the Summerside Journal-Pioneer that I have deliberately mislead this House, I ask you, Sir, to let me read from an editorial of October 10 from Summerside's The Journal-Pioneer entitled, "An Apology and Clarification from Minister McKnight is now in Order". I will read one part. "Speaking of an error in judgment perhaps The Journal-Pioneer learned a lesson as to how not to do things in the future. If one is going to reprint an editorial from another newspaper that is opposite of the editorial stance, and in this case, The Journal Pioneer, one should choose carefully the position on the editorial stage to which to reproduce that editorial. If it is reproduced at the top left-hand side of the page under editorial heading, then perhaps there should be a lead paragraph emphasizing that the comments are being reflected and reflect the editorial position not of The Journal Pioneer. Perhaps more than one credit line should appear throughout the reproduced editorial so there would be absolutely no doubt that the editorial was being reproduced from another newspaper."
I believe that the hon. member who read his question into Hansard may wish an opportunity to observe what he said. Again, I emphasize that I have no problem whatsoever with the hon. member putting forward a position on behalf of his constituents, but I do request that the rules and traditions of this House be maintained.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Earlier today in the Question Period the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion made a mis-statement. I said that he misled the House- and I did not say at the time when I raised it whether it was deliberate or otherwise-when he said that the rules
October 13, 1989

in place in automotive trade between Canada and the U.S. today are the same as they were in 1965.
That, of course, as I pointed out in my question is totally false. They were changed.
