speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TABLING REPORT OF THE COMMISSION TO REVIEW ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32(1), I have the honour to table in the House, in both official languages, a report of the Commission to Review Allowances of Members of Parliament.
As has been the custom in the past, I would presume that this report be referred to the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services pursuant to Standing Order 32(5).

Routine Proceedings

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32(2), I wish to table at this time, in both official languages, copies of the government's draft legislation for the proposed goods and services tax and comprehensive explanatory notes.
This document fully reflects, in draft bill form, what the August technical paper would look like if it were put into bill form. I am tabling this document simply to fulfil our promise made in August when we released the technical paper to do so.
By translating the technical design of the proposed GST into legal language, the draft legislative provisions elaborate on the mechanics of the proposed tax and give greater precision to its operational detail.
As we indicated this summer, this is a further step in the GST consultation process and will assist the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as well as the professional community in their study of the GST technical paper.
To be clear, this is not a bill introduced into the House. That step must await the government's consideration of the report of the finance committee on the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, since my appointment as Minister of State for Housing, I have always been concerned about the problem of affordable housing. I try to help prospective homeowners and Canadians who are having trouble becoming homeowners.

We are all aware that some housing markets, such as the greater Toronto area, are overheated with demand outstripping supply. There is a serious affordability problem within the Toronto region and an important factor in this is the limited supply of suitable land available for housing.
Some months ago the federal government announced that 50 hectares, that is 135 acres of surplus federal lands at the Downsview Airport site in North York would be made available for housing, and at that time Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the federal housing agency for which I am responsible, was given the responsibility for the development of that site.
Yesterday, I had the honour of announcing that the federal government has released another major site within the greater Toronto area in order to help address the housing needs of the region. The surplus land which the federal government is releasing on this occasion is a parcel of approximately 43 hectares, 106 acres. It is located in the town of Vaughan. This is expected to provide for up to 2,500 new homes.
Again, in keeping with the government policy with respect to the Downsview lands, it is our intention to serve a wide range of types of households. I anticipate that the new neighbourhood will be the home of between
6,000	and 8,000 people. The federal government expects that at least 25 per cent of the homes will meet the needs of young couples just starting out, of senior citizens and of disabled persons. What CMHC is striving for is an income-mixed community, providing a broad range of housing forms.
I might just say at this point that certainly that 23 per cent figure is a minimum, as I indicated in Question Period, but it remains to be worked out with the town of Vaughan as to the exact mix and the exact kind of community.

The federal Government will develop this land in close co-operation with the Town of Vaughan, the York region and the Ontario government, to ensure that this project is a success and benefits all concerned.

The town of Vaughan has been most interested in how this land would be developed since the time that it was declared surplus by Environment Canada with the decision to relocate the facilities of the Atmosphere Environment Service. I have therefore offered my assurances to the mayor and members of the Vaughan council that we will be working closely with them and their officials toward the realization of common objectives.
October 13, 1989



This land is being released as part of the Government's current policy of better management and reducing its land holdings, while taking steps to meet the housing needs of Canadians. These measures have made individual parcels of land available, like the Downsview property which CMHC is now developing.

As I have said since I was appointed Minister of State with the responsibility for housing, I have been looking for ways to address the very urgent needs for affordable housing in certain high-cost areas of our country. It was for this reason that I was particularly pleased to make this announcement. For me this is another step which I hope will bring really tangible results.
I want to thank my colleagues in the government for making this possible. It is a product of co-operation as well as a reflection of our commitment to sound management and the leadership role we are playing in housing in Canada.
The release of the Vaughan land is a result of a CMHC analysis of the development potential of the site which was conducted for the Treasury Board with the support of Public Works Canada. If we are to meaningfully deal with the housing needs of Canadians it will require the same spirit of co-operation on the part of all levels of government as well as from private and nonprofit sectors, indeed from all Canadians.
At this time I would like to invite all Canadians to make their concerns known to individual members of Parliament and to the Government of Canada with respect to housing.
I would like to add special thanks to some of my colleagues, including the President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. Robert de Cotret, the Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Elmer MacKay, all the Treasury Board Ministers, my colleagues in the cabinet from the Toronto region, the Hon. Michael Wilson, the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Barbara McDougall, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Hon. John McDer-mid, the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization,
Routine Proceedings
and to say that this would not have happened without their help and co-operation.
One other very brief point I would like to make, Madam Speaker, is to point out and congratulate a former member of this House, the former member for Willowdale, John Oostrom, who played an important role in bringing this particular parcel of land to the attention of the House some many months ago. If it had not been for Mr. Oostrom's efforts at that time this land undoubtedly would not have been used for housing, and I think it is appropriate that we all express our thanks to John Oostrom and to all of our colleagues who have played a part in this announcement of yesterday.

Madam Speaker, the decision announced by the Minister of State for Housing regarding the transfer of the Vaughan lands is to be applauded. The principle of surrendering unused government lands for housing development must be encouraged. It is unfortunate that no action is being taken elsewhere in the country where the needs are also acute.
In his statement the minister states that he is concerned about the problem of affordable housing, but nothing in his announcement guarantees that a good portion of these new homes will respond to that very need. What will these homes cost? What type of homes will they be? For whom are they really intended? How does the minister define affordable housing? There is no indication except to parrot what has been said, very properly, in Ontario. How much real consultation has there been with the municipality? The question is, what is the substance behind this announcement?
For several weeks now the Liberal task force on housing has been covering the country. Everywhere we have gone groups have denounced this government's withdrawal, its lack of interest in housing, its obvious lack of leadership in solving what is a fundamental crisis of poverty, affordability and accessibility in the country, the budget cuts which have crippled Canadians who seek affordable housing and the high interest rates which have added and exacerbated the very real problem.
For example, last spring this government announced the end of the rental program, the RRAP. This program was vital in order to renovate the existing low quality housing stock in the country. It was a program vital to allow families to live in decent and affordable housing.

Routine Proceedings
No government which cut that basic program can claim to have any interest in the housing crisis in this country.
When I heard of the most recent announcement-I understand the Minister made many references to Downsview and I wish I could quote his comments on the lack of attention to Downsview when he was a private member as opposed to the minister-it really did bring to mind the inaction of this government. In that case, despite the statements, the good intentions, the laudable declarations, the heartfelt promises that we have heard, not one thing has been done. Not one unit has been constructed. Not a thought has been given to sewage systems or any of the tremendous costs of providing infrastructure. We do not know who is going to develop the land, who is going to pay for it or who is going to supervise it. This government makes announcement after announcement and then does nothing about it. There is no execution, no implementation because there is no commitment to solving the problem.
Is this what is in store now, Madam Speaker, for the Vaughan land? Must the community simply sit around and wait as people have waited for the Downsview implementation? When are we going to see something concrete coming out of this announcement? What Canada needs is a comprehensive housing policy that recognizes the real needs of this country. The government's decision to apply this land is one we all welcome, but it must ensure that it is done within the framework of a coherent policy, one that responds to the expectations of the people and to their socioeconomic problems.
[Translation}
Madam Speaker, Canadian men and women need affordable housing. The Government's programs should be aimed at filling this need.

Madam Speaker, I am new to this House, and I guess I am a little bewildered. I had thought minister's statements were used to announce significant policy changes or significant programs, not used to do basically a small PR job which was already done in a press conference yesterday.
The minister has announced the release of the Downsview lands on which there are going to be 600 affordable houses. Canada has 1.2 million children living in poverty. Canada needs 100,000 affordable houses built every year, this year, next year, for the next five years, and the minister is announcing 600.
When asked by the press how he defined affordable houses he said, $150,000 to $200,000. What are we talking about in affordability? He has made no commitment that any of the 600 units will, in fact, be non-profit housing or co-op housing. He says that the government is going to meet the 25 per cent minimum required by Ontario. Where is government leadership? Why is the government not talking about 50 per cent or 75 per cent of the housing being affordable? We have a serious problem in this country. Thirty per cent to 40 per cent of Canadians do not have access to affordable, good quality housing. There are 1.2 million children living in poverty, and the minister is talking about fiddling around with 600 housing units.
When I heard yesterday that the minister was going to make a statement I thought we were going to have a statement that the government was embarking on a bold program that was going to attack the question of affordability of housing across Canada.
The Canadian Real Estate Association says there are 27 regions in this country which have severe affordability problems. The minister has made two peanut announcements dealing with one of them, in his own backyard of Toronto. This does not do anything for people in Edmonton, Calgary, Halifax or Vancouver.
There is an increasing question of credibility emerging around the Minister of Housing. When he was a backbencher he spoke eloquently. Since he has become minister he has taken no action. His announcement is like someone sitting on a sinking ship and bailing with a teacup-it is not even a teacup, it is a spoon.
Six hundred units of affordable housing does nothing to alleviate the problem across this country. I had hoped he was going announce a program where interest rates or mortgages were going to be reduced by 4 per cent, or that the government was going to fund municipal infrastructure, or triple or double the number of co-operative or non-profit housing, or bring in his favourite pet, a
October 13, 1989

speculators' tax which he advocated before he was a minister or restore the RRAP program. But we heard about none of these.
I am left with a bewildered feeling, and I think most housing organizations in Canada are being left with that same feeling. Where is the leadership? Where is the commitment? How long is the minister going to think that platitudes and inaction are going to really solve the problem?

I do not know how government members felt that day, but I think a number of members on the opposition side felt betrayed by the actions of the minister. Three government members rose to speak that afternoon. I suspect that government members felt very awkward having defended the agency that afternoon in the House of Commons.
They went through that exercise, explaining the need for that agency, only to find out that their minister, a minister from Nova Scotia, was in a committee room of this House saying that for budgetary reasons the agency was going to have to use its money over a much longer period of time, effectively reducing the amount of money available in each and every year for the next five years.

October 13, 1989
Private Members' Business
Obviously the demands which the members of all three parties had spoken about with some eloquence were not going to be met.
Since that time other announcements have been made by this same minister which have restricted the ability of the Atlantic agency to deal with the problems in that region. I remember the member for St. John's East getting up and saying that it is very important that decisions be made in Atlantic Canada by Atlantic Canadians. He made that one of the focal points in challenging the motion I had put before the House.
What I find interesting is that not only did the minister cut the funding which the Tory members had found to be so important for Atlantic Canada, he decided without consulting the board to change the criteria with regard to whom and what corporations are eligible for funding.
Let me explain that. Under the new criteria only certain firms will be eligible for funding. Only proposals that would require funding for over $200,000 would be eligible for grants. Well, that is a change in the emphasis of the program. It was a change made by the minister and by his officials in Ottawa; not by people in Atlantic Canada; not with the knowledge of the Conservative MPs, I suspect; not with the knowledge of the Conservative Premier of Nova Scotia; not with the knowledge of the people who are on the board, the people who are supposed to be "making the decisions on behalf of Atlantic Canada, by Atlantic Canadians", to quote Conservative members.
I am quite interested to hear the speeches later today to see what the minister might do to reverse himself yet again in the future.
I wanted to speak seriously about the importance of providing more funding to Atlantic Canada and how important it is to restrict through change the program criteria that the minister announced last spring.
One of the documents I want to refer to is a leaked document prepared by the Nova Scotia Government. It reads:
ACOA's focus on very small companies weakens the ability of the province to attract medium and large industrial development.
That is a quote from the Nova Scotia Conservative government's response to what the federal Conservatives have done. In other words, it has said that the new criteria restricting the funding to less than $200,000 is
preventing development of medium and large operations in Atlantic Canada.
It is not a New Democratic statement. It is not a statement on behalf of the Liberal party. It is a statement of the Nova Scotia Conservative government attacking the cut-backs and the change in criteria made by the minister responsible. I have forgotten his riding, but it used to be represented by the Prime Minister when he was looking for a seat before he received a seat in Quebec.
I remember going out to campaign against him in the by-election. One of the things the Prime Minister said at that time was; "Elect me and we will look after you. Elect me and I will make sure that the concerns of Atlantic Canadians are on the front burner. Elect me and I will make sure that you have the funding that you need".
That is not what the government of Nova Scotia or the Premier of Nova Scotia who campaigned for the Prime Minister in those days are saying. They are saying that by cutting back the funding, restricting the amount of money that is available and changing the criteria you are preventing Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, P.E.I, and "the rock" from developing in the way that they need to develop.
Let us look at the other cut-backs. Which part of the country was hurt most by the VIA cuts? Atlantic Canada. Where does the most vociferous protest come from with regard to the cuts? Atlantic Canada. Which area has improved its usage of VIA in response to the Deputy Prime Minister's challenge? It was Atlantic Canada. Which area of Canada feels most betrayed by this government with regard to the VIA cuts? Again it is Atlantic Canada.
Let us consider other areas of economic development. The federal government basically announced this fall that there will be half as much money for tourism in Atlantic Canada as there was in the past, in an area which is starting to boom, where there is growth. There are more American tourists coming up and more Canadians going to Atlantic Canada. This is a sector which employs people, where small businesses do very well, where the local communities all benefit, and the federal government says: "We are cutting that back".
Not only is it cutting it back by half but it has decided that from now on it will not be a separate fund. It has to come from the funding for ACOA. In other words, the
October 13, 1989

funds that were just cut on May 15 not only have to cover all existing programs, all existing requests, but now have to look after tourism as well because tourism will not be a separate development.
I had a press conference on these issues in September and I called it a triple whammy. The federal government is socking it to Atlantic Canada time after time after time, and it is doing all it can to make sure that the economy of Atlantic Canada is devastated by the budget measures of the Minister of Finance.
After being betrayed by their own Prime Minister and by their own cabinet minister, I wonder how Conservative members of Parliament will have the courage to get up yet again in this House and say that my motion is going in the wrong direction.
How will they be able to say that the federal government, the federal Conservatives would never hurt Atlantic Canada? The last time they got up to speak, to defend their minister, to defend their Prime Minister at the same time, without telling them the minister was down the hall in a committee of this House taking money from Atlantic Canada. He was taking money that had been promised to Atlantic Canada, taking money that was supposed to be part of an agreement with Atlantic Canada. He said: "You are not getting it in the next three years. We will give you the same amount over the next five years". I do not know how some of those Conservative back-benchers feel, but I suspect they feel betrayed.
Certainly their constituents feel betrayed. Certainly there is a growing feeling in Atlantic Canada that they are being ignored. It does not matter whether it is the fisheries. It does not matter whether it is tourism. It does not matter whether it is those people who rely on VIA Rail. It does not matter whether it is the seniors who look at their pension plans being eroded by this government. There is a very strong growing sense that this government has ignored, betrayed and is abandoning Atlantic Canada. That feeling was there. I do not think any Conservative member is going to deny that feeling because it is growing and they must be hearing it back home.
Private Members' Business
What I am calling for in the motion is a positive approach. First, we have to get rid of the cut-back mentality of the federal Conservatives. In its place we have to make sure that those agencies which are established actually have the power to make decisions affecting Atlantic Canada, and that those decisions are, again to quote the Conservatives, "Made by Atlantic Canadians". That is not happening. The area feels devastated.
The government is producing programs which are hurting people in that region. The government is showing it has absolutely no concern for Atlantic Canada. What we need is a statement by this House in the form of a motion which I hope the Conservative members present can support. It is a votable motion. We can vote on it if the Conservatives agree to it. We can vote on a motion that states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider
the advisability of providing long-term regional planning for the
Atlantic region through an expanded Atlantic Canada Opportunities
Agency.
This is not a motion condemning the government. This is a motion giving direction to the government. This is a motion saying that we want an expanded role. It does not even mention extra money, only an expanded role. It calls for "long-term regional planning", and it explains that the agency that should do so is the very agency Conservative members got up and spoke about with such eloquence just a few short months ago.
I do not want to take all the time available in this debate. I want the Conservative members here to have a chance to explain why they too support this motion and why they too believe that we need an expanded role, that we need long-term regional planning for Atlantic Canada, and that we cannot have a continuation of the betrayals of the Prime Minister and the betrayals of the minister responsible for the agency as we have had in the past.
We no longer want to be in a situation of such short-term planning as we had in the past where a Conservative member is speaking in defence of an agency in the House, not knowing that the cabinet minister is down the hall cutting the funding for that agency. Stand up for your region, stand up for funding for Atlantic Canada, stand up for long-term planning for that region.

October 13, 1989
Private Members' Business

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT ATLANTIC CANADA OPPORTUNITIES AGENCY
speechtext:
Speaker, I rise with great pleasure today to participate in this debate. I thank the hon. member for Churchill for providing an opportunity for myself and other members of the House to get up and talk about the excellent things that are being done by this government in Atlantic Canada.
The member's motion calls for long-term planning. That is precisely the role that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency plays. He calls for an expanded Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. There is absolutely no question that the overwhelmingly positive response that has been received from business across Atlantic Canada to ACOA means precisely that it is an overwhelming success, and I hope some day we will find more funding.
It is a fact that $1.05 billion were committed, were made available, by this government. In the first two years $600 million of those dollars were committed already and in this year $400 million will be spent by ACOA. This indicates that the government in fact has a very impressive record in Atlantic Canada and that this government has and will continue to have a very substantial commitment to Atlantic Canada and to long range planning for Atlantic Canadians.
Needless to say, as with any agency there is an ongoing review and dialogue taking place. As new needs occur they will be responded to, and I was particularly pleased to see this government's response earlier this year to the burgeoning crisis in the Atlantic fishery in setting up a special cabinet committee which will assist ACOA and other agencies in responding to the needs of Atlantic Canada.
ACOA, quite simply, is an Atlantic Canadian success story. It has been a tremendous value to the economy and to the people of Atlantic Canada. I might say, Madam Speaker, that credit for this has to go to the individual whose vision led to the establishment of ACOA, and that is the Prime Minister of Canada. We as Atlantic Canadians and I as a member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada, and I am sure my colleagues on this side from Atlantic Canada, are proud to stand with that Prime Minister and recognize the leadership he has provided in bringing about ACOA and the fact that he knows our region so well.
We have also benefited I might say from leadership from three ministers-the minister from the other place, the Minister for Federal-Provincial Relations, the now Minister of Veterans Affairs, and indeed the current minister of ACOA, a man who I might say is probably as well respected and popular as any person in the province of Nova Scotia for the leadership that he has provided many, many years in this Parliament, in the governments of Canada, and the tremendous leadership that he has provided for our province.
ACOA's staff have worked diligently. The problem that the 300 people who work for ACOA have had has been keeping up with the volume and demand for the opportunity to participate in the many programs of ACOA. I look forward to ACOA playing a very positive role under its new president, Mr. Lesault, who I know will maintain the quality of leadership that we have had from ACOA.
The basis of success of ACOA, unlike any other regional development program to date, is the fact that ACOA is based in Atlantic Canada and the decisions for ACOA are made in Atlantic Canada. ACOA, naturally as an agency of government, receives its funding from the government of Canada.
Just as any other department of government, decisions are made by cabinet, funds are allocated, structures are created. The significant thing about ACOA is that it is based in Atlantic Canada. The project decisions and the various other co-operative efforts in which ACOA gets involved are made by Atlantic Canadians in Atlantic Canada. There is nowhere in Canada where there are people with greater initiative, greater energy or better ideas than the people of Atlantic Canada. The result is that we are seeing on a daily basis the benefits coming from the 1.05 billion new dollars that were brought in.
My hon. friend made reference to a document that was released in Nova Scotia. I am sure that it was not his intention to in any way mislead this House by suggesting that it was a document of the government of Nova Scotia.
I just want to set the record straight. The Minister of Development of the province of Nova Scotia commissioned a study of ACOA by an outside person, a professor from Acadia University who did a study and submitted it to the government of Nova Scotia. In the opinion of the minister it was so outrageous that he sent
October 13, 1989

it back and refused to accept the document. He suggested that there be more facts and less opinion in the document.
Instead of revising the document, as should have been done, he released it to the New Democratic Party. The Leader of the New Democratic Party of Nova Scotia got up and made all sorts of statements about ACOA based on a document that had been rejected. It was indeed not the document of the Government of Nova Scotia. I think we should refer to that as the document of the New Democratic Party of Nova Scotia. It is not by any means a document of the Government of Nova Scotia.
The action program of ACOA has had a profound impact in supporting new ideas, expanding businesses and facilitating the diversification of industry throughout Atlantic Canada. It has been particularly helpful to small business. It has also been beneficial to large businesses.
From time to time people ask me why the government makes grants to business. Are business people not wealthy? Why do they need money from the government? People do not understand that the role of an industrial incentive program is to make things happen where we want them to happen, in this case in Atlantic Canada as opposed to other places. Funding and support through the various means that come with the action program means that industries and expansions happen in Atlantic Canada and not somewhere else where they might otherwise happen. That is the concept of incentive.
If ACOA makes a contribution to the development of a business, it is only a contribution towards that happening. They are not giving money to somebody. They are creating opportunities for Atlantic Canada. The people who own those businesses make investments. They are no more interested in losing on their investments than are the Government of Canada or the people of the maritimes in terms of those investments. We have to understand that the benefit that comes back is a benefit to all Atlantic Canadians. In employment opportunities the money eventually comes back to the government through taxation and through expenditures in those communities. Everybody wins all around.
Private Members' Business
Reference was made to the suggestion that the ACOA decisions are made in Ottawa rather than in Atlantic Canada. Decisions in ACOA are made by a highly competent team of public servants. Some people suggests that ACOA decisions are made by politicians. There are times when it might be very helpful to me and some of my colleagues from Atlantic Canada if we had funds to dispense for encouraging businesses and so on. It does not work that way. Everything is done above board. Decisions are made in accordance with clearly established criteria.
Suggestions are made with respect to the fact that there has been a modification in the process by which ACOA's funds are being spent. Members opposite seem completely unaware that in this country we have, as a result of many years of overspending, a serious debt problem. All Canadians are aware of that debt problem. All areas of government have to participate in dealing with that debt problem. All regional development agencies in Canada, as with all other aspects of the government, have had to participate in coming to grips with this.
The important thing to note is that the money that was committed at the beginning of ACOA is still there. The $1.5 billion to assist in job creation in Atlantic Canada is still there. It will be spent in Atlantic Canada for the benefit of Atlantic Canadians.
I recall last spring when the budget came down hearing from members opposite that there would be no money for other regional development. The term "cut" is constantly used. They said there would not be any money for ERDAs or co-operative agreements. It is interesting to note that the minister responsible has now reached agreements in all four Atlantic provinces.
Newfoundland recently announced agreements for coastal Labrador and rural development.
Several agreements in principle have been reached in Prince Edward Island. One was the signing of a $25 million agri-food agreement.
A package of agreements involving a commitment of $97.7 million by the Government of Canada in New Brunswick, including a $32 million agri-food agreement, was signed by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Veterans Affairs just last week.

October 13, 1989
Private Members' Business
In my province of Nova Scotia we now have five co-operative agreements, including a $200 million-plus agreement to deal with the Halifax harbour pollution problem, an agri-food agreement and most recently, forestry, fishery and mining agreements.
Between ACOA and these co-operation development agreements, this government has committed over $2 billion to regional development in Atlantic Canada. It is indeed a very impressive record.
I have no reservations at all in going back to Atlantic Canada as a member of Parliament in support of this government. No government in the history of this country has done as much for Atlantic Canada as this government is doing and will continue to do.
In closing, I want to quote from a statement made by the Prime Minister of Canada in Halifax this summer. He said: "ACOA is about the future, about helping business people improve productivity, exploit new technology, develop new markets and create new jobs. ACOA represents a new approach and a new commitment on our part to Atlantic regional economic development".
That approach is working. That commitment is producing results. ACOA is here to stay and our government commitment, reinforced by success, is even greater.
Atlantic Canada and Atlantic Canadians have never been better served than they are being served and will continue to be served by this government.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT ATLANTIC CANADA OPPORTUNITIES AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise and speak in this debate concerning the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
You are no doubt aware, Madam Speaker, that Atlantic Canada depends heavily on federal regional development assistance. Indeed, the federal government established ACOA to help alleviate the economic disparity which has plagued Atlantic Canada.
However, in looking at ACOA's record I cannot help but feel that the agency possesses serious shortcomings. The motion put forward by the member for Churchill states veiy clearly that the government ought to consider implementing long term regional planning in Atlantic
Canada by expanding the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
While the motion seems very good, and I can very easily support it, the truth is that although ACOA was launched by the Conservative Government amid a great deal of fanfare, it has fallen far short of the mark. My hon. colleague from the other side quotes the right hon. Prime Minister. I have a quote here also.
When addressing the Saint John Board of Trade in October of last year, the Prime Minister said: "The federal government has a responsibility for regional development in the interests of national unity and as well in the interest of fairness. We will not have two Canadas in the economic sense anymore than in the constitutional sense. We will not have one Canada that is prospering at the centre while other regions do not receive a fair share of economic opportunity".
They are great words. Everyone in this House I am sure would agree with them. They sound fantastic. But words are cheap.
Let us look at what the government has been doing not only to Atlantic Canada but right across the country. First, there is VIA Rail, the recent announcement by the Minister of Transport on VIA Rail, the cut-backs. We look at the new proposed tax. Speaking of taxes it is this very same government that increased taxes 31 times since 1984. The hon. member talked about the deficit, the debt. Since 1984 this government has doubled it. We talk about UIC and the changes proposed to it. Again, it is going to affect Atlantic Canada.
The hon. member from the other side sort of praised ACOA and all its benefits. To be honest, there are some benefits to ACOA. There is no doubt about it. We need ACOA. We need other programs as well. But there are some problems with ACOA. There are some problems with the direction the government is going in.
I have a few articles. I want to point out some of the headlines that have come out since the budget and since the announced cut-backs to ACOA. What amazes me is how members on the government side seem to say that ACOA has not been cut. Well, here are a few headlines with regard to statements made by the hon. minister responsible for ACOA.
October 13, 1989

One is from The Toronto Star. It states: "Ottawa slashes Atlantic funding". The article is about the proposed changes in ACOA.
Here is another one from a local paper in New Brunswick. It states: "ACOA cuts called sell-out of Maritimes".
I have another one which states: "Tories to slash cash for regions by $2 billion". Down below there is a little sub-article entitled: "Budget leak suspect may not be charged".
Another article states: "Ottawa cuts Atlantic Canada development aid", again referring to the hon. minister and his program of spreading the same amount of money over a period of seven years rather than the original five years.
Here is a good one, Madam Speaker. It states: "Half-baked ideas and half-measures". There is a big question mark there. They are talking about the regional development policies of this government.
Another one states: "Atlantic Canada, the nation's economic wasteland gets wasted again". The article goes on to explain how Atlantic Canadians are not being treated fairly or equally, as the Prime Minister indicated it should be throughout Canada.
Madam Speaker, I have another article here from VAcadie nouvelle, New Brunswick's francophone newspaper, and the headlines are incredible: The ACOA has no way of knowing whether the funding it provides is spent on the projets submitted. All this doesn't make sense. The article quotes the Minister responsible for ACOA as saying: We don't have the financial and human resources for providing follow-up. A projet follow-up would be very expensive, and I am not convinced it would be worthwhile.

The minister is telling us in his own words that they have no way of checking to see if the money that he is giving out through ACOA is actually being spent on those projects. He says: "We do not have enough personnel, and even if we did, I do not even know whether we would check. It may not be a good idea".
I want to go to a more localized problem that has been underlined just recently in my own riding. The article that I am referring to is an article that appeared in a local
Private Members' Business
paper of the city of Campbellton. The headline here states: "ACOA tactics jeopardizing developments in Ccunty". The mandate of ACOA was to develop industry, to develop enterprises. The article goes on to quote the industrial commissioner of the Restigouche Industrial Commission. This is a neutral group, a group that has the good of the region in mind. It is a group that is trying to do exactly what ACOA is doing.
Here is what the industrial commissioner had to say: "Clients have been kept waiting for months. We are being kept in the dark and they have made so many changes to the program, it is unbelievable". That is what the industrial commissioner in one of the regions in New Brunswick is saying.
Another point that the article goes on to explain is that the old mistakes of changing the regional policies in mid-stream is creating havoc. It is the same old problem that we have had before whereby the government announces a program. It sounds great. There is a big fanfare. The Prime Minister gives a big speech. A year or so down the road, there is a change. They have all sorts of reasons. There is the debt, the deficit, whatever, all sorts of reasons that they can well explain.
I should also point out to show the seriousness of it-and I do not want to discuss the case-that ACOA is being taken to court in the region as well because of problems created by the agency.
When we look at ACOA in general, it sounds as if I am very critical of it. I am. I am critical because it should have been a good tool. It should have been the answer to our problems. But it is not. There are a lot of problems with the ACOA program as it now stands.
One of the things that I want to point out is that I am not criticizing the personnel. The personnel are doing their best at whatever they do, whenever they do it. They do not have the backing of this government. That is the problem. They do not have enough personnel or the finances.
When we talk about a long range plan, this government has no long range plans. It has no long range for anything in Canada, let alone for Atlantic Canada. Maybe the motion should have been expanded to include other areas. They have been in government since 1984, which is actually too long. They have ruined the economy. There is no doubt about that. They are ruining the transportation system across Canada. Now they want to investigate it while they are ruining it. When the investi-

October 13, 1989
Private Members' Business
gation is over, we are just going to find out that it is ruined. It will be too late.
I have a few constructive ideas, if hon. members are listening. Perhaps we could increase the personnel of ACOA. Another constructive idea is to go back to the original five-year commitment, rather than a seven-year commitment.
One other thing that I should point out, and the hon. member opposite also mentioned it, is that decisions for ACOA are made by civil servants. The new president of ACOA has already stated publicly that the $200,000 limit on the action plan was a mistake. Let us see that changed as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT ATLANTIC CANADA OPPORTUNITIES AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in the debate this afternoon. As a member from Atlantic Canada, I have watched over the years a state of economic decline, fortunately reversed by the government elected in 1984. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that I serve with a great deal of enthusiasm as the member from Fundy-Royal, and I am in total support of the types of policies that this government has initiated over the past five or six years.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the mover of the motion, as well as to my hon. colleague from New Brunswick, the member for Restigouche- Chaleur. I must say that I find a similarity that develops among opposition members that is rather strange, particularly in view of the historic relationship that the party of the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur had with Atlantic Canada, which was to put it into a desperate state of morass and decline for all of those years when they were in charge. The correlation that I draw between the two members' speeches is that it is more significant of what they have not said, as opposed to what they did say.
It is to the credit of this government that in a period when restraint is obviously the key word-and it is difficult to find funds of any significance to go into disadvantaged regions, such as Atlantic Canada-that this government was able to come up with in excess of $1.2 billion for a program of great vision through the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency when previous administrations were able to do nothing but recycle old
funds again, again, and again, of dollars going into Atlantic Canada. There have been thousands of jobs created. Hundreds of families which were previously disadvantaged and are now able to provide themselves a decent standard of living, something which before just simply did not exist.
I want to remind you that it was not that the previous administration had not attempted from time to time to deal with the discrepancies and the disparities in Atlantic Canada because, indeed, it paid lip-service. The disturbing thing is that during a great deal of that time the party of the member who moved the motion, the NDP, was supporting and propping up the Liberal government which continued to contribute to such a deplorable state of the economy in Atlantic Canada.
I think it is important to recognize that there are some substantial developments over the last few years that perhaps are not given the profile they deserve.
I want to talk particularly about education and research. My hon. colleague from South Shore only had a short time to deal with some of the problems and some of the positive things that have taken place with reference to his area. Education and research are as important to Atlantic Canada as it is to the rest of the nation.
The best and the brightest of young Atlantic Canadians are often forced to leave home. We saw a lot of that during my earlier years when it was the norm that young Atlantic Canadians left Atlantic Canada. I had to leave Atlantic Canada because I was unable to find a job. Many hundreds and thousands of other young people during that period of time found themselves in the same situation. They are often forced, even today, to leave home to seek opportunities elsewhere. However, that is changing because of the initiatives and the foresight of this government.
The region which has been deprived of the talent, ambition and vigour of part of its younger generation, could not possibly continue to survive under those types of conditions. Atlantic Canadians, like all Canadians, are loyal to the province of their birth. Given equal opportunity they would gladly stay home and participate to make whatever contribution they could to its wealth. Part of
October 13, 1989

ACOA's task, as this government saw and perceived it, was to give them the opportunity to do just that.
Let me mention today just a few of the projects, particularly in the field of education, which are being or will soon be undertaken with at least partial funding, if not total funding, from ACOA that will make it possible for Atlantic Canada's brightest and best to stay at home, to grow and to contribute.
The programs designed to educate the next generation of entrepreneurs must be effective. We must first describe the strengths and weaknesses of the present public school system and university curricula and we must do this in relation to the field in which the initiative is directed. By so doing we can discover how the educational system can foster entrepreneurial spirit by teaching the necessary appropriate skills.
Entrepreneurship Project, PEP, is a research program undertaken jointly by Mount Allison University and the Universite de Moncton. Its work will establish what attitudes toward and conceptions of entrepreneurship are prevalent in the school system, both among students and teaching personnel; what courses and entrepreneurial skills are being offered and how they are taught; how school curricula may be modified to give the students the opportunity to increase their knowledge and ability in the field of business development; and how the subject of entrepreneurship is treated in the teacher training institutions.
PEP is designed to attack the roots of the economic problems in the Atlantic provinces. New products, new production methods and new markets do not create themselves. They are created by people but people need the tools to exploit those opportunities, to discover new products and markets. ACOA believes that PEP is Canada with the tools they need to achieve economic equality with the rest of Canada.
Another project which complements PEP at the university level is the establishment at the University of New Brunswick of a chair of technological management and entrepreneurship. Too often, students of engineering and other applied sciences, while well educated in their particular discipline, receive no training whatsoever in the entrepreneurial skills which would enable them to exploit to the fullest, and to the benefit of their commu-
Private Members' Business
nity as well as themselves, the practical knowledge they have gained at the cost of long, hard studies.
Innovative ideas, because of the lack of ability to create a market for them, are lost. The chair of technology management and entrepreneurship will develop courses designed to give these students the business development skills to complement their scientific knowledge. The University of New Brunswick will assume the funding and ensure the continuation of the chair of technology management and entrepreneurship after ACOA funding for the project expires.
In addition, a chair of international marketing has been established at the Universite de Moncton. This chair is also partially funded by ACOA in collaboration with the province of New Brunswick and the private sector. Once again, the university will pick up the funding after the ACOA program expires.
Telemedicine and Educational Technology Resources is a joint project of the Telemedicine Centre and the School of Continuing Studies of Memorial University of Newfoundland. The goal of this project is to establish and operate a facility providing a network of educational communications, using the latest electronic technology, throughout the province of Newfoundland.
The communications network will be capable of delivering training programs to remote areas of that province. These programs will be directed toward a variety of groups, including industry, business and professional associations, as well as community groups and others requiring specialized training.
There is one industry which is important equally to all of us in Atlantic Canada and that is the one of tourism. In fact, it is an important source of revenue for all of Canada, both provincially and federally. In the Atlantic provinces it is equally important. It is certainly an important employer.
Therefore, ACOA is proud to contribute, in co-operation with the province of Nova Scotia, the private sector, and Mount Saint Vincent University, to the funding of an expansion of the tourism and hospitality degree program offered by that university.
These are just some of the education projects that ACOA is working with and developing in Atlantic Canada. I would like to say, in closing, that I am convinced ACOA will continue to build on the excellent

Private Members' Business
start it has made and it deserves the continued support of the people it serves and the support of this Chamber.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT ATLANTIC CANADA OPPORTUNITIES AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, like my hon. colleague who just spoke, I also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon. I think that if we look at past events and consider other regional development programs introduced by this Government since 1984, it is all very reminiscent of our Plan de Vest in the Gaspe, in Eastern Quebec. I think we can find a parallel with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, in the way it works in disadvantaged areas where a tool is needed, as the Hon. Member said earlier. In order to stimulate the economy in our regions, it is very important that the federal Government be able to provide, not only human resources, but also the funding we need to develop our own economy as we see fit. With the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, we already have some concrete examples. We can talk about Cape Breton Island, where Micronav Ltd. will create 120 new jobs providing systems for airports throughout our country and even internationally. Madam Speaker, I think it is important that all Canadians understand that in regions like ours, the Atlantic, the West, the Far North, new technology will help us provide more jobs for our youth and we have something to offer.
Also, Madam Speaker, for sure not all Canadians want to live in Montreal or Toronto. Programs like ACOA in the Atlantic today are the way to keep our young people where they live.

It is very nice for the opposition always to shoot and attack.
I am very familiar with the Atlantic region. My colleague mentioned Mount Allison University. I was fortunate enough to have good professors and I graduated from there many moons ago. I am glad to see that that university is taking part in the ACOA program.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT ATLANTIC CANADA OPPORTUNITIES AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak again on ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, in this House. My hon. friend across the way keeps coming up with suggestions for ACOA that are inherent in ACOA today. I need not remind hon. members that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is the first attempt, after a number of attempts by a variety of governments, to deal specifically and effectively with the problems of regional development in Atlantic Canada.
The fundamental problem with programs in the past has been that the direction, the policy framework, and the decisions came from the centre, from here in Ottawa. I need not remind any member in this House of the problems of developing policy inside across the country. There have been problems. ACOA is so successful, as my friend from the South Shore has pointed out, because the decisions are made in the region by people from the region who are dealing every day with the problems, the challenges, the innovations, the imagination of people in the region. It has four components. The first is action and we have seen that in the action plan. The second is co-operation. The third is co-ordination and the fourth is advocacy.
I think it is important to get on the record the success of ACOA, what ACOA has been able to do in the 19 or 20 months since it has been active. Up until early September ACOA had approved 6,336 projects, committed $607 million and leveraged, seen other people invest, $1.7 billion. That is co-operation. That is using federal government programs and federal government resources to generate other resources, to increase in-

vestment in co-operation with the people who live and work in the Atlantic provinces. We have helped to create 16,714 jobs and maintain another 18,936 jobs. Those are results. That is progress. In 19 months of existence, close to 70,000 inquiries have been received, 13,000 applications have been received; 10 times the rate of any other program.
The other thing that I think is particularly important is to recognize that what has happened in the last 19 or 20 months is that this government has provided more funding assistance to assist business than has been provided in the last 25 years. If that is not results, if that is not commitment, if that is not progress, then, Madam Speaker, I do not know what is.
We have, as my hon. friend has said, seen 22 new co-operation agreements put in place. We have seen the federal government sitting down with the individual provinces and saying: "Okay, what is important to you is to develop in the longer term the economic base of your province, and how can we, as the federal government, with our money, with our knowledge, with our expertise, help you do that?"
We have seen 22 new co-operation agreements; $274 million, and there are more to come. That is one of the roles of ACOA in developing and providing that long term strategic approach-that hands-on at the table, what's the problem, how are we going to solve it, approach-to try to deal with economic development, job creation and expansion in the Atlantic provinces.
Seventy-five per cent of the approved projects of ACOA had a capital investment of less than $200,000; small projects, one or two people, six or seven people, maybe much larger but the government's participation was much less smaller, or that was what was asked for. Twenty-two per cent were from that level up to $2 million.
Two of the missions of the agency, two of the things that the agency is said to have to deal with, are co-ordination and advocacy. Unfortunately, you do not see that all the time. There are not press releases, there are not news clips. You do not see it every day as you walk down the street as sometimes you do with new plants and new jobs. I see it all the time in my dealings in Newfoundland and Labrador in how we come to deal with our problems. ACOA is at the table dealing with the challenges that we have in the short term and in the long term with our fish problem, in advice to the Clark committee, in active,
Private Members' Business
strong participation with the Stein group. Hibernia and offshore oil development has the full participation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. They are providing the big picture. They are providing the longer term view. They are providing the other side to economic development as opposed to just the immediate problem at hand.
The youth strategy is such a critical step to dealing with the long term problem that the young people in my province have had in getting from school to work. ACOA is playing a substantial role in how to make that happen, not only in providing advice, but in bringing together other departments of this government and of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador with the people dealing with the youth strategy and with the private sector. How can we deal with the problem together in the longer term? How, over time, can we attack the problem of young people not being suitably employed, young people not getting from school to work? What is the problem? How do we get through it? We see it in forestry.
I had the privilege of being at the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council meetings last week in Moncton where the new president of ACOA, Mr. Leseau, who has been referred to here today, is bringing a fresh approach. He recognizes clearly and stated before these people that we have a particular challenge and that ACOA has a role to play in developing a strategy. ACOA has a role to play in moving the Atlantic provinces ahead. That role that this motion calls for is very much there with the vice-presidents and with the people who work for them in each of the regions.
A number of my colleagues have been able to illustrate projects which have been very successful. There is one that I am very proud of and that is a project sponsored by the Newfoundland and Labrador Status of Women's Council under the direction of Anne Bell and the participation of people like Wendy Williams.
What we are doing through that program is saying, her e is $800,000 plus-I think that is the right number-go out and hire people. They will hire six people to work as field workers. Women are badly under-represented in this economy and badly under-represented in the Newfoundland economy, and there is no question that they have a huge contribution to make, not just to women but to the whole economy and to the whole society. But women are not getting taken care of by the system. Their ideas and their innovations are being lost.
